dedupe_keys.name: united states economy wide impacts of a hypothetical african swine fever outbreak

description: This case study uses a computable general equilibrium (CGE) model to estimate how a hypothetical African swine fever (ASF) outbreak would ripple through the United States pork supply chain, the wider economy and international trade. The authors, researchers at Colorado State University, Kansas State University, Texas A&M University and the Roslin Institute at the University of Edinburgh, published it in an open-access journal article. Four scenarios vary outbreak size and export restrictions; the model adjusts production, prices, bilateral trade flows and welfare, and robustness is checked with systematic sensitivity analysis. Coverage is national for the US with global trade effects. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Caveats: the outbreaks are hypothetical, and CGE results depend on the base-year data and elasticities. The study found that small outbreaks cause limited disruption and US welfare losses of 310 to 563 million dollars, while large outbreaks cut US hog production by 7.34 to 8.57 percent, raise hog producer prices by about 42 percent, reduce GDP by 0.05 percent and cause welfare losses of 10.9 to 11.4 billion dollars, with trade shifting to other exporters. Simulation uses: shock scenarios for food supply resilience and cascading economic impact models. Related records: the GTAP Data Base (data-gtap-data-base) is the kind of global trade database such CGE models are built on, and the H5N1 dairy study (case_study-us-h5n1-dairy-outbreak-economy-wide-cge) applies the same approach to another animal disease.
